question: What explains the change in checkout latency during this time window?

timeline_observations.statement: Checkout service version eval-20260920T141549-v1 logged startup with pool_size=10 and db_work_seconds=0.2.
Mean checkout request duration in the 2026-09-20T14:16:00Z bucket was 0.207082 seconds.
Checkout service version eval-20260920T141549-v2 logged startup with pool_size=2 and db_work_seconds=0.2.
Mean checkout request duration rose to 0.592762 seconds in the 2026-09-20T14:17:00Z bucket and 1.03257 seconds in the 2026-09-20T14:18:00Z bucket.

Mean connection wait time rose from 0.000288413 seconds in the 2026-09-20T14:16:00Z bucket to 0.386186 seconds in the 2026-09-20T14:17:00Z bucket and 0.826957 seconds in the 2026-09-20T14:18:00Z bucket.

Pool utilization for version eval-20260920T141549-v1 reached a maximum ratio of 1.0 (fully occupied) in the 2026-09-20T14:16:00Z bucket, and version eval-20260920T141549-v2 reached a maximum ratio of 1.0 in both the 14:17 and 14:18 buckets.

leading_hypothesis.statement: A new checkout process (version eval-20260920T141549-v2) started with a much smaller connection pool (pool_size=2 versus the earlier pool_size=10). Under concurrent traffic the smaller pool became fully occupied, so requests spent most of their time waiting for a connection, which explains the rise in checkout latency; the latency increase is almost entirely accounted for by increased connection wait time rather than slower query work.
verification_needed: Retrieve traces from the degraded interval to confirm requests were served by the v2 process and that waiting, not slower database work, dominates span time.
Confirm the intended pool configuration for the v2 version and whether the pool_size=2 startup reflects a deliberate change.
Confirm which process versions were actually serving traffic during the degraded buckets.

supporting_findings.statement: Mean checkout request duration increased from 0.207082 seconds in the 2026-09-20T14:16:00Z bucket to 1.03257 seconds in the 2026-09-20T14:18:00Z bucket.
Mean connection wait time increased from 0.000288413 seconds in the 2026-09-20T14:16:00Z bucket to 0.826957 seconds in the 2026-09-20T14:18:00Z bucket, accounting for most of the latency increase.
Version eval-20260920T141549-v1 logged startup with pool_size=10 and db_work_seconds=0.2; version eval-20260920T141549-v2 later logged startup with pool_size=2 and db_work_seconds=0.2.
Pool utilization for the v2 process reached a maximum ratio of 1.0 (fully occupied) in the 14:17 and 14:18 buckets.
Checkout request rate peaked at a sample mean of 31.6394 requests/second in the 14:16 bucket, showing concurrent load during the latency rise.
The configured db_work_seconds was 0.2 at both startups, while observed request duration exceeded 1.0 seconds, indicating the added time is not configured query work.

contradicting_findings.statement: Version eval-20260920T141549-v1 also showed full pool utilization (ratio 1.0 maximum) in the 14:16 bucket while latency was still low, so full utilization alone does not explain the degradation; the pool size change and rising wait time do.

missing_information: No traces were retrieved, so per-request breakdown of wait versus query execution time is unverified.
No pool_limit metric series was supplied, so the observed pool sizes come only from startup logs, not a configuration metric.
It is not confirmed which process versions were serving traffic in the degraded buckets or whether the v1 process stopped.
The log search for "limit" returned no events; absence of limit-related logs does not confirm configuration intent.
recommended_next_steps: Retrieve traces from the degraded interval to confirm connection wait dominates request time and identify the serving version.

Consider a controlled test restoring the connection pool size to 10 (the value observed at the earlier startup) and verify whether connection wait and latency return toward baseline; this is a proposal, not an executed change.
Confirm the intended pool configuration for the new version and whether the smaller pool was deliberate.
Determine how many checkout process versions were serving traffic during the incident window.
